title: Evidence for Interleukin-17C governing interleukin-17A pathogenicity and promoting asthma endotype switching in bronchiectasis

paper_content.abstract: The management of bronchiectasis-asthma overlap (BAO) is an important clinical issue to be addressed. Little is known regarding the endotype of BAO. Here we recruit patients with a primary diagnosis of bronchiectasis and co-existing asthma. The levels of interleukin (IL)-17C are positively correlated with the levels of IL-17A or group 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s) in peripheral blood samples from patients with BAO. An in vivo mouse model of Pseudomonas aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection followed by ovalbumin-induced asthma shows that IL-17C potentiates IL-17A expression via interacting with IL-17 receptor E in ILC3s. Additionally, ablation of Il17re in mice attenuates ILC3 responses and IL-17A-mediated asthma endotype switching towards neutrophilic asthma driven by P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection. Lastly, impaired epithelial barrier integrity by P. aeruginosa exposure is associated with IL-17C production in vitro. Collectively, our study implicates evidence for IL-17C governing IL-17A pathogenicity and promoting asthma endotype switching in bronchiectasis, implicating IL-17C as a potential therapeutic target for individuals with BAO.
paper_content.introduction:
Non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis and asthma exhibit the same degree of heterogeneity in terms of clinical manifestations and outcomes1–4. Based on the related immune-inflammatory pathways, asthma endotypes broadly cover three subgroups: type 2-high, type 2-low, and mixed endotypes. Type 2-high asthma is characterized by a predominance of eosinophils, while neutrophilic asthma is typical of type 2-low asthma5, where with release of cytokines such as interferon (IFN)-γ, interleukin (IL)-17 from T helper (Th)1, Th17 cells, group 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s) to recruit neutrophils and dampen the acquisition of eosinophils6–9, type 1 and type 3 immune responses predominate, leading to the suppression of type 2 immune responses10. In clinical practice, bronchiectasis and asthma frequently coexist, however, it is uncertain whether there is a cause-effect relationship between these two disorders. The overlap between bronchiectasis and asthma can be viewed as asthma-bronchiectasis overlap (ABO), and bronchiectasis-asthma overlap (BAO) with asthma accounting for 3-8% of bronchiectasis cases11–14, which are both clinical issues. The endotype of BAO has yet to be deciphered, and identifying the underlying mechanisms is therefore of key importance in precision medicine. Moreover, managing patients with BAO poses challenges, particularly when it comes to the use of corticosteroids. Inhaled corticosteroids and conventional asthma therapy are not regularly recommended for treating bronchiectasis, as the potential inhibition of host immunity and further increased risk of infections1,15. The conflicting treatment approach poses a significant challenge for healthcare providers. Literature on BAO is still scarce16,17, and the endotype of BAO remains to be fully defined, which has become a barrier to treatment decision-making. Furthermore, the lack of a mature animal model mimicking BAO has limited the availability of basic research data. Notably, Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common pathogen in the lower respiratory tract among bronchiectasis patients2,18, and it is also an independent risk factor for acute exacerbation in bronchiectasis16. And P. aeruginosa chronic infection model has been widely used in a repertoire of research on bronchiectasis19–21. Recent studies have indicated that colonization of nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae promotes the development of Th17-related neutrophilic asthma with glucocorticoid resistance22,23. Both P. aeruginosa and nontypeable H. influenzae belong to Gram-negative bacteria, but the precise asthma endotype which P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection drives remains unclear.

Innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) comprise group 1 ILCs (ILC1s), group 2 ILCs (ILC2s), and ILC3s, share the same features as three major effector CD4+ Th subsets, including Th1, Th2, and Th17 in the expression of transcription factors and cytokines, and act as pre-primed effector cells without de novo antigen-triggered effector cells differentiation24–26. The IL-17 family consists of six structurally related members (IL-17A, -17B, -17C, -17D, -17E, -17F). IL-17A and IL-17F are released by immune cells, mostly including ILC3, γδ T17, Th17 cells, and signal through IL-17 receptor A (RA)/IL-17RC and IL-17RA/IL-17RD complexes, and thus participate in host defense, inflammatory diseases, and autoimmune disorders partly by mediating neutrophil accumulation6,7. Other IL-17 members -IL-17B, IL-17C, IL-17D, IL-17E- contribute to regulating tissue inflammation by interacting with receptor complexes in epithelial cells or specific lymphocyte subsets27–30. However, the involvement of IL-17A, IL-17C, and ILC3s in the induction and development of endotypes within the context of BAO has not been deciphered.

In this work, we report a model of P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection followed by ovalbumin-induced experimental asthma mimicking BAO to investigate the underlying mechanisms involved in the endotype of BAO. This study indicates evidence for IL-17C governing IL-17A pathogenicity and promoting asthma endotype switching in bronchiectasis, implicating IL-17C as a potential intervention target for individuals with BAO.
paper_content.results:
Exposure to P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection drives asthma endotype switching towards neutrophilic asthma associated with Th17 cells and ILC3s
In the present study, 20 healthy controls (HC), 31 bronchiectasis patients, 30 asthmatics, and 31 patients with BAO were enrolled. And as shown in Supplementary Table 1, there was no obvious significance concerning the sex distribution and the percentages of participants with smoking history across the groups (P=0.1643, P=0.4304). Patients with BAO had worse lung function, as indicated by lower FEV1, FVC, FVC% pred values, lower scores on Asthma Control Test (ACT), lower levels of eosinophils and higher percentages of IgE to be below 100 compared to asthmatic patients, but there was no significance of FEV1% pred, FEV1/FVC, fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) values in patients with BAO (Supplementary Table 2). These characteristics suggested that BAO may tend to be type 2-low asthma with poor control.

As described in Fig. 1a, consistent with patients with a primary diagnosis of bronchiectasis and coexisting asthma within the context of BAO, we established a model of P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection through intratracheal (i.t.) instillation with P. aeruginosa-laden agar beads, followed by ovalbumin (OVA)-induced asthma to explore the specific endotype of BAO. Considering P. aeruginosa clinical strains are more efficient in building chronic infection compared with the PAO1 laboratory strain31, we confirmed a slower growth rate of 52D5 compared to another three existing clinical strains isolated from bronchiectasis patients in our lab (Supplementary Fig. 1a), and therefore adopting the 52D5 clinical strain in the subsequent experiments. To improve the efficiency of airway colonization with P. aeruginosa, we constructed the agar beads of diameter ranging between 100 and 200 μm31. Additionally, compared to sterile agar beads, P. aeruginosa-laden beads seemed denser as shown by visible single bacterial cells interiorly (Supplementary Fig. 1b). The establishment of chronic infection was successful as determined by recovery of more than 1000 colony forming units (CFUs) of P. aeruginosa from lung cultures32 at different time points post infection (Supplementary Fig. 1c). There was no significance of survival rates post infection between P. aeruginosa and P. aeruginosa/OVA (PA/OVA) group (Supplementary Fig. 1d).

Hematoxylin & eosin (HE) staining showed more marked peribronchial infiltration of inflammatory cells in treatment with OVA, PA, and PA/OVA compared to controls (Fig. 1b, c). Moreover, airway resistance was pronouncedly augmented in mice exposed to PA/OVA compared to mice exposed to phosphate-buffered saline/OVA (PBS/OVA) (Fig. 1d). And the levels of serum IgE and Th2-related cytokines IL-5, IL-13 in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) were reduced in mice exposed to PA/OVA compared to PBS/OVA, whereas the concentration of IL-17A was increased (Fig. 1e–h). Consistent with pathological presentations, the total cell numbers in BALF were elevated in mice exposed to OVA, PA, and PA/OVA (Fig. 1i). Furthermore, as depicted in Fig. 1j, the cell percentages and numbers of eosinophils whether in BALF or in lung tissues from PA/OVA group were consistently reduced compared to PBS/OVA group, whereas the cell percentages and numbers of neutrophils were elevated and the cell counts of alveolar macrophages (AM) were comparable (Fig. 1k–p). These findings suggested that exposure to P. aeruginosa chronic infection drove the asthma endotype switching towards neutrophilic asthma.

It is known that Th2 cells, together with ILC2s, contribute to eosinophilic asthma by producing IL-5 and IL-1333,34, while IL-17A-producing cells such as Th17, γδ T17, and ILC3 cells contribute to airway neutrophilia via IL-17A6,7,35,36. Consistently, compared to PBS/OVA exposure, PA/OVA exposure resulted in mitigated Th2 cell responses and upregulated Th17 cell responses (Fig. 2a–d). Additionally, through the assessment of ILCs based on the expression of transcription factors or cytokines, we found that the cell percentages and counts of ILC2s were consistently reduced in mice administered with PA/OVA in comparison with PBS/OVA-exposed mice, whereas ILC3s elevated (Fig. 2e–l). Meanwhile, with the determination of ILC2s based on cellular surface receptors, exposure to PBS/OVA increased the levels of ILC2s, whereas exposure to PA/OVA decreased (Supplementary Fig. 2a–c). The percentages of IL-17A-producing cells among CD3+CD4- lymphocytes which might be regarded as γδ T17 cells were increased in PA/OVA-treated mice compared to PBS/OVA-treated mice, but the cell numbers weren’t affected (Supplementary Fig. 2d). Additionally, mRNA level of Il17a was also significantly upregulated in lungs of mice administered with PA/OVA compared to PBS/OVA (Fig. 2m). Notably, we found no pairwise significance of the levels of Th1 and ILC1 cells among four groups (Supplementary Fig. 2e–g). Consistently, human data also indicated that patients with BAO presented higher levels of ILC3s compared to asthmatic patients or healthy participants (Supplementary Fig. 2h). Additionally, in line with the reported link of P. aeruginosa infection to Th2 responses37,38, our data showed raised TSLP in P. aeruginosa-infected patients with bronchiectasis or BAO, whereas no significance of CCL-17 levels was observed (Supplementary Fig. 2i, j). Thus, exposure to P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection led to a shift in asthma endotype towards neutrophilic asthma associated with IL-17A-producing Th17 cells and ILC3s.

IL-17A mediates asthma endotype switching towards neutrophilic asthma driven by P. aeruginosa chronic exposure
To understand the role of IL-17A in asthma endotype switching, an IL-17A neutralizing antibody (anti-IL17A) was administered to determine whether P. aeruginosa exposure-driven asthma endotype could be rescued as depicted in Fig. 3a. The administration of anti-IL17A attenuated peribronchial infiltrates of inflammatory cells and epithelium thickening induced by PA/OVA exposure, however, the effect was not observed in OVA group (Fig. 3b–d). Furthermore, IL-17A neutralization led to a mild increase in the levels of IgE, IL-5, IL-13, eosinophils, Th2 and ILC2 cells, whereas a significant decrease in the levels of IL-17A, total BALF cells, neutrophils, Th17 and ILC3 cells in the PA/OVA group (Fig. 3e–n and Supplementary Fig. 3d, f). Moreover, although the administration of anti-IL17A augmented the ratio of AM from mice treated with PA/OVA, the total numbers of AM, Th1, and ILC1 cells weren’t affected (Supplementary Fig. 3a–c, e). Taken together, these findings demonstrated that IL-17A mediated a shift in asthma endotype towards neutrophilic asthma driven by P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection.

Epithelial barrier integrity is impaired in a P. aeruginosa-exposed asthma model
Previous studies have reported the defective epithelial barrier integrity among patients with asthma39,40. Consistent with the mouse model, following pre-stimulation with P. aeruginosa, A549 cells were treated with OVA or IL-13 to resemble the airway epithelium within the context of BAO. We found that PA/OVA or P. aeruginosa/IL-13 (PA/IL13) exposure resulted in marked morphological changes in A549 cells from a typical multilateral paving stone-like appearance to a round or fusiform appearance accompanied by protrusions (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 4a). Furthermore, exposure to PA/OVA or PA significantly increased the intercellular permeability compared to OVA treatment (Fig. 4b). Moreover, the mRNA and protein levels of tight junction (TJ) markers, ZO-2, ZO-3, Claudin-18 and adhesion junction (AJ) marker, E-cadherin were remarkably decreased after PA/OVA or PA/IL13 exposure compared to OVA or IL-13 exposure (Fig. 4c–l).

Airway epithelium, as the first line of the physical barrier in the host, produces several alarmins such as TSLP41. Here we observed that exposure to PA/OVA or PA/IL13 augmented Tslp expression compared to the administration of OVA or IL-13 (Fig. 4m), which corresponds to the upregulated TSLP expression in human corneal epithelial cells exposed to P. aeruginosa infection42. In addition, the expression of ZO-3 and Claudin-18 located at the most apical part of neighboring epithelial cells were both decreased in the lungs of mice exposed to PA/OVA compared to OVA or their control (Fig. 4n, o and Supplementary Fig. 4b, c). Altogether, P. aeruginosa exposure resulted in a loss in epithelial barrier integrity characterized by the increased intercellular permeability and the decreased cell-cell adhesions.

The level of IL-17C positively correlates with IL-17A and is associated with the defective epithelial barrier integrity
Given the critical role of IL-17A in the model, we further explored the potential upstream regulator of IL-17A expression. Previous researches have demonstrated that IL-17C or IL-17B can regulate the activation of Th17 cells via a direct or indirect manner27,29,43,44. Moreover, IL-17B can inhibit eosinophilic inflammation by antagonizing IL-17E (IL-25) expression associated with type 2-high asthma45,46. We then examined the expression of IL-17 family members in P. aeruginosa chronic infection-driven asthma model. We found that Il17c expression was significantly upregulated in lung tissues of PA/OVA group compared with OVA group, whereas no significance of Il17b, Il17d, and Il25 mRNA expression was detected (Fig. 5a–d). Meanwhile, we observed significantly elevated expression of Il17c followed by remarkable upregulation in Il17a expression at the indicated time points in lung tissues of mice initially exposed to P. aeruginosa infection compared to their control (Fig. 5e, f). Furthermore, compared with OVA exposure, PA/OVA exposure elevated the concentration of IL-17C in BALF (Fig. 5g). Consistently, we found more productions of IL-17A and IL-17C in serum from patients with BAO than asthmatics (Fig. 5h, i). Notably, there was a consistently positive correlation between IL-17C and IL-17A levels (Fig. 5j). More importantly, IL-17C levels were also positively correlated with ILC3 levels in patients with BAO (Fig. 5k).

In line with animal and human data, IL-17C expression was upregulated in both BEAS-2B and A549 cells exposed to medium with a certain concentration of OVA following P. aeruginosa pretreatment (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b). Additionally, exposure to PA/OVA or PA/IL13 induced significantly elevated the expression of IL-17C compared to the treatment with OVA or IL-13 (Fig. 5l–o). MMP-9, secreted partly from neutrophils, is reported to modulate epithelial junction integrity47. Interestingly, exposure to PA/OVA or PA/IL13 expressed more Mmp9 than OVA or IL-13 administration (Fig. 5p, q). Notably, the pretreatment of MMP-9 inhibitor HY attenuated the impaired epithelial integrity and the upregulation of IL-17C expression induced by PA/OVA or PA/IL13 exposure (Supplementary Fig. 5c, d and Fig. 5r–u). Together, MMP-9 could modulate epithelial barrier integrity and thus regulating IL-17C expression.

Collectively, these data indicated that the levels of IL-17C positively correlated with IL-17A or ILC3 levels. Defective epithelial barrier integrity was associated with IL-17C production via MMP-9-dependent manner.

Ablation of Il17re inhibits IL-17A production in neutrophilic asthma driven by chronic infection with P. aeruginosa
It is known that IL-17C signals through IL-17RA/IL-17RE complex48. To investigate the potential role of IL-17C in asthma endotype switching, airway inflammation was evaluated in Il17re-/- mice. Exposure to PA/OVA exhibited milder peribronchial inflammatory infiltrates in Il17re-/- mice than wild-type (WT) littermates, but ablation of Il17re didn’t affect inflammatory infiltrates in the OVA group (Fig. 6a–c). Compared to WT littermates, CFU counts in the whole lung were markedly decreased in Il17re-/- mice exposed to PA/OVA or PA (Fig. 6d). Moreover, ablation of Il17re reduced the levels of IL-17A, total cell numbers, the cell counts of neutrophils, Th17 and ILC3 cells in mice exposed to PA/OVA, but failed to impact the levels of IL-5, IL-13, eosinophils, Th2 and ILC2 cells other than a mild increase in IgE levels (Fig. 6e–p and Supplementary Fig. 6b, c). In addition, total numbers of AM were not affected by ablation of Il17re (Supplementary Fig. 6a). Lastly, we found that interfering Il17c expression amplified the upregulated expression of Tslp in exposure to PA/OVA (Fig. 6q). Collectively, these data indicated that ablation of Il17re attenuated neutrophilic airway inflammation driven by P. aeruginosa chronic infection by preventing IL-17A production derived from Th17 cells and ILC3s.

IL-17C binds directly to ILC3s through interacting with IL-17RA-IL-17RE complex in lung tissues and potentiates IL-17A expression
To investigate the mechanisms by which IL-17C regulates IL-17A expression in ILC3s, we initially searched for the potential signaling targets in ILC3s. Interestingly, according to published RNA-seq data49, a significant increase in the expression of Il17re and Il17ra was supported in ILC3s of small intestine from WT mice, with Cd93 and Vipr2 expression being positive controls, but small amounts of transcripts expression of other IL-17R family members Il17rb, Il17rc, and Il17rd were observed (Fig. 7a). We observed that IL-17RE was situated on the surface of ILC3s and 98.9% among sorted ILC3s were RORγt+ (Fig. 7b–d). Next, we validated the binding capacity of IL-17A or IL-17C to ILC3s and identified more IL-17C or His labeling IL-17C binding to ILC3s, whereas ablation of Il17re attenuated the binding capacity (Fig. 7d, e). Furthermore, we found that following IL-17C treatment, ILC3s from C57BL/6 mice, compared to those from PBS-injected control mice, showed the elevated expression of IL-17A, whereas the comparable expression of the other transcripts associated with ILC3 function (Fig. 7f–h and Supplementary Fig. 7a–c). Moreover, we discovered that IL-17RE expression was comparable among ILC3 cell populations, whereas IL-17RE+ ILC3s expressed more IL-17A than IL-17RE- ILC3s in lung tissues (Supplementary Fig. 7d and Fig. 7i, j). Lastly, we found that IL-17RE was mostly expressed in T cells, macrophages/dendritic cells (MΦ/DC), and ILC3s (Supplementary Fig. 7e). Collectively, these findings indicated that IL-17C can interact with IL-17RE in ILC3s and potentiate ILC3 responses.
paper_content.methods:
Patients’ samples collection
Humans samples were collected from healthy participants, patients with asthma, bronchiectasis, or BAO in Shanghai Pulmonary Hospital. The diagnosis of asthma was based on the Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) guidelines64. Asthma control was assessed using the ACT score. The diagnosis of idiopathic bronchiectasis was referred to the non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis guideline published by the British Thoracic Society in 201965. Patients with BAO met one of the following diagnostic criteria: (1) Bronchiectasis was clinically reported prior to asthma; (2) Asthma was newly diagnosed according to the bronchodilator reversibility test on the basis of a primary diagnosis of bronchiectasis. Patients with cystic fibrosis or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) were excluded from the study. Participants without respiratory symptoms and an indication of acute, active, as well as chronic pulmonary lesions were recruited as healthy controls. The clinical characteristics of the patients and healthy controls are shown in Supplementary Table 1. Study protocols for research related to human samples, including informed consent, publication of demographic data, and associated corresponding source data, were approved by the ethics committees of Shanghai Pulmonary Hospital (approval number K21-318). This study was conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki principles, and signed informed consent was obtained from all participants.

Mice strains and animal experiments
Il17re-/- mice (Il17retm1Lex/Mmucd) on B6N.129S5 background were provided by Prof. Youcun Qian, Chinese Academy of Sciences. C57BL/6 mice were bought from Shanghai SLRC Laboratory Animal Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). All mice were maintained in specific pathogen-free animal facilities with a 12-h light and dark circle, temperature of 20–25°C, and relative humidity of 50% at the Laboratory Animal Center of Tongji University. All animals were age-matched and sex-matched, and then randomized into different groups. The age for all strains of mice was 6–8 weeks. OVA-induced asthma is known to result in eosinophilic inflammation and induction of Th2 cytokines in BALF. To construct a model of P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection followed by experimental asthma mimicking BAO, following i.t. instillation with P. aeruginosa-laden agar beads (2×106 CFUs in 35 μl PBS) to establish chronic infection with P. aeruginosa31, 5 days later Il17re-/- mice and wild type (WT) littermates or C57BL/6 mice entered into the establishment of an experimental asthma model66, in which intraperitoneal injection of 20 μg of OVA (Sigma-Aldrich) mixed with 2 mg of alum (Thermo Scientific) was given, followed 6 days later by continuous three airway challenges with 1% OVA. For IL-17A neutralization, 30 μg of Anti-IL17A (BE0173, BioXcell) or IgG1 isotype control (BE0083, BioXcell) was intratracheally given into the four groups, that is, PBS, OVA, PA, and PA/OVA at 2 h before airway challenge with 1% OVA. For IL-17C administration, 1 μg of IL-17C (2306-ML, R&D) or PBS was intratracheally instilled into C57BL/6 mice every 2 days for a total of five times. All mice were sacrificed 24 h post the last airway challenge or the last instillation via isoflurane inhalation, and samples, including serum, BALF, and lung tissues, were collected for further analysis. Apart from the quantification of IgE in serum and the assessment of indicators, including bacterial load, IL-17 expression, immune and inflammatory cell infiltrates in lung tissues, the levels of IL-5, IL-13, IL-17C, IL-17A, and cell typing were determined in BALF. Experiments were conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki conventions for the use and care of animals and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Tongji University (approval number TJBE00120101).

Measurement of AHR
In PA/OVA-induced airway inflammation model, changes in AHR after allergen exposure were determined by invasive measurement using R&C system (EMMS). At 9 days post OVA sensitization, the trachea was intubated, and then the lungs were mechanically ventilated. Airway resistance was regarded as an indicator of AHR and measured after increasing doses (0, 16, 32, 64, 256 mg/ml) of aerosolized acetylcholine chloride (Ach, A6625, Sigma-Aldrich).

Cell culture and treatment
The A549 lung epithelial cell line (SCSP-503, Chinese Academy of Sciences) and BEAS-2B bronchial epithelial cells (SCSP-5067, Chinese Academy of Sciences) obtained from the Chinese Academy of Sciences, were both cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM, Gibco) containing 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco). Unless otherwise indicated, P. aeruginosa clinical strain 52D5 was employed in the subsequent experiments. Following pretreatment with live 52D5 (multiplicity of infection (MOI)=1) for 5 h, the previous medium was replaced by medium containing OVA at various concentrations (50, 100, 250 μg/ml) or added with exogenous IL-13 (PeproTech, 100 ng/ml). Finally, cells and supernatants were both collected for further analysis after incubation at 37°C for 24 h. Il17c small interfering RNA (siRNA) used in the experiment was synthesized by GenePharma, and the sequence (5′–3′) was as follows: GCGAGACAGCUGCGCUCAACU; UUGAGCGCAGCUGUCUCGCGG. For Il17c siRNA transfection in A549 cells, GP-transfection-Mate (G04008, GenePharma) was used following the manufacturer’s instructions. For the inhibition of MMP-9 in A549 cells, cells were primed with the inhibitor (HY-135232, MCE, 50 μM) for 2 h before P. aeruginosa stimulation.

Bacterial growth curve
Growth rates of P. aeruginosa strains were assessed as described by Montanari67. Briefly, P. aeruginosa strains were grown overnight in Luria-Bertani (LB) broth (12780052, Invitrogen), and each culture was diluted at 1:200 and standardized to an OD600 in the range of 0.01 to 0.02. Samples were taken every 0.5 or 1 h and the OD600 was determined. Growth curves were plotted according to the elapsed time and the corresponding OD600 value.

Bacterial culture and preparation
The P. aeruginosa clinical strain 52D5 was thawed from −80°C, cultured in LB broth overnight, and then re-grown for 8 h at a diluted factor of 50 to reach the mid-log phase. Finally, Bacteria were washed and resuspended in PBS for cell pre-stimulation. P. aeruginosa-laden agar-beads were made as described previously31. Briefly, a 1:9 (v/v) mixture of bacterial suspension and melting broth was added to heavy mineral oil (330760, Sigma-Aldrich) that was equilibrated at 55°C, rapidly stirred for 6 min at room temperature, then cooled 35 min at 4°C, followed by washing six times in PBS. CFUs were enumerated on an aliquot of homogenized bead slurry via a 10-fold serial dilution. Sterile beads were prepared using PBS.

Quantification of bacterial loads in lung tissues
The whole lung tissue was removed and then homogenized in 1 ml of sterile PBS. And 0.1 ml of the homogenate was transferred for a 10-fold serial dilution, followed by inoculation on the LB agar plates. Finally, bacterial colonies were counted after incubation at 37°C for 24 h.

Lung histology
Lung lobes were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, then embedded in paraffin and sectioned, followed by HE staining. An individual blinded to experimental conditions assessed airway inflammation. The average of histological scoring on airway inflammation by randomly selecting five visual fields of each lung section from at least three mice per group under a light microscope (Olympus) was used for further analysis.

Quantitative real-time PCR
Total RNA was extracted from cells or lung tissues using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) according to the instructions, followed by reverse transcription using a cDNA synthesis kit (Yeasen). qPCR analysis was performed with a SYBR RT-PCR kit (Yeasen) on LightCycler 480 (Roche). Gapdh was used as an internal reference gene for data normalization. The primer sequences were shown in the Supplementary Table 3.

Western blotting
The samples were separated by electrophoresis through a 4–12% Precast Bis-Tris gel (Tanon) and electrically transferred to PVDF membranes (Millipore). The membranes were blocked with 5% fat-free milk, followed by incubation with the primary antibodies at 4°C and secondary antibodies at room temperature, as well as repeated washes with TBST solution (0.1% Tris, 0.1% Tween-20). And finally, proteins were visualized using Tanon imager.

ELISA
IL-17A, IL-17C, TSLP, CCL17 in human samples and IgE, IL-5, IL-13, IL-17A, IL-17C in mouse samples were measured using an ELISA kit as shown in the Supplementary Table 4. Assays were referred to the manufacturer’s protocols.

BALF collection
The lavage fluid was collected with 0.4 ml sterile PBS injected into the whole lung each time for a total of three times, immediately stored in ice, and then centrifuged at 350×g for 7 min. The supernatants were maintained at −80°C for cytokine assays. The cell pellets were removed of red blood cells, re-suspended in PBS, and then taken out an aliquot for cell number counting. Finally, the remaining cell suspension was prepared for flow cytometry analysis.

Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) isolation
PBMCs were isolated from the peripheral blood samples collected from the recruited participants with Ficoll Paque PLUS (GE healthcare) using density gradient centrifugation layering according to manufacturer’s protocols. Cells were suspended with a centrifuge at 350×g and then stored in −80°C for further flow cytometry analysis. Human sera were available by centrifuging at 3000 rpm and were also stored in −80°C for cytokine assays.

Flow cytometry analysis
Lung tissues of the indicated mice were prepared into a single cell suspension with the digestion buffer (sterile PBS supplemented with 2.5 mg/mL type 2 collagenase, 1% DNase I). After red blood cell lysis and filtering, cells were centrifuged, and subsequently pellets were suspended with 30% (v/v) Percoll solution (GE healthcare). After centrifuging, cell pellets were washed and re-suspended in sterile PBS containing 3% (v/v) FBS, 0.05 mM EDTA, 100 U/ml penicillin, and streptomycin. An aliquot of suspension was used for cell number counts, and the remaining cells were stimulated with a cell activation cocktail with Brefeldin A (Biolegend) for 4 h prior to staining for flow cytometry analysis by CytoFLEX LX (BECKMAN COULTER). Additionally, fluorescein-conjugated antibodies against CD45 (30-F11, 103116), Lineage (17A2; RB6-8C5; RA3-6B2; Ter-119; M1/70, 133310), CD90.2 (30-H12, 105305), RORγt (AFKJS-9, 12-6988-82), GATA3 (16E10A23, 653806), T-bet (4B10, 644806), EOMES (W17001A, 157703), CD127 (A7R34, 135022), CD3 (17A2, 100218), CD4 (GK1.5, 100443), IL-5 (TRFK5, 504306), IL-13 (W17010B, 159403), IL-17A (TC11-18H10.1, 506930), IFN-γ (XMG1.2, 505806), IL-17RE (944904, FAB7997R), His (J095G46, 362605), IL-17C (311522, IC23061R) were purchased from Biolegend, eBioscience or R&D. Cell surface staining was carried out by incubating cells with the antibodies for 30 min at 4°C after blocking with Fc antibody. GATA3, RORγt, T-bet, EOMES, IL-17A, IL-5, IL-13, and IFN-γ staining was performed using the intracellular transcription factor kit (Invitrogen) or the cytokine staining kit (BD Biosciences). For flow cytometry sorting of ILC3s, FACSAria III (BD Biosciences) was employed in the experiment. The detailed reagents were shown in Supplementary Table 4. Flow cytometry data were analyzed with FlowJo software (v10.7.2)

Immunohistochemistry Staining
Lung sections were completely immersed into Tris-EDTA (pH=8.0, Servicebio) or citric acid (pH=6.0, Servicebio) antigen retrieval solution and then heated with a microwave for 15–20 min, followed by blocked by 3% hydrogen peroxide for 15–20 min. After 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) blocking, the sections were incubated with antibodies against ZO-3 (Invitrogen) or Claudin-18 (Abcam) at 4°C overnight, followed by colorimetric detection using DAB staining and hematoxylin counterstaining. The sections were examined using a light microscope and quantified by the Image-Pro Plus 6.0. An individual blinded to experimental conditions performed a semiquantified analysis.

Immunofluorescence microscope
Sorted ILC3s from lymphoid cells were cultured on poly-L-lysine-coated plates and were then fixed and blocked with 5% (v/v) goat serum (Yeasen) in PBS for 1 h at room temperature, followed by incubation with an antibody against IL-17RE (bioss) at 4°C overnight. Subsequently, the cells were stained with DAPI (Beyotime) for 5 min at room temperature. Cells were rinsed with PBS for three times, 5 min each time. Images were captured under a Zeiss fluorescence microscope (Zeiss).

Binding assay

The Shapiro-Wilk test was employed for analyzing the distribution of quantitative variables. Normally distributed data were presented as mean (SD), or mean ± SEM, and non-normally distributed data were presented as median (IQR). Spearman correlation was used to investigate the relationship between the level of IL-17C and IL-17A or ILC3s in serum from patients. This study by Zhang et al. addresses current challenges in the treatment of patients with coexisting bronchiectasis and asthma. The authors sought to explore the asthma endotype in patients with non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis with asthma (BA) to identify new therapeutic targets. Using mouse models, the authors report a pathogenic interaction between IL-17C and ILC3s that potentiates IL-17A responses and switching to a neutrophilic asthma endotype. The study is interesting and warrants investigation, however, there are some major limitations.
- The authors’ rationale for inducing P. aeruginosa infection followed by allergic sensitisation to Ova in their murine model lacks convincing justification. While individuals of all ages can have bronchiectasis, it is most common in the elderly. The EMBARC study explored this overlap between asthma and bronchiectasis and identified that asthma could be reported as an etiology of bronchiectasis. This is supported by the British thoracic society guideline for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis recommendation for considering asthma as the cause of bronchiectasis in the absence of other etiological explanations. Others show that asthma severity is an independent risk factor for bronchiectasis, that there is a high percentage of bronchiectasis in patients with severe asthma, and that age of asthma onset and exacerbations are independently associated with the occurrence of bronchiectasis.
- Does P. aeruginosa infection alone adequately model the diverse immunopathological repertoire and pathophysiology of patients with bronchiectasis? This must be established to convince readers that the reported observations are not simply readouts of host:pathogen interactions e.g. the effects of an active infectious challenge on shaping allergic sensitisation and the immunological profile of the recall response.
- The potential influence of smoking history on the reported data is not discussed further than reported rates of “Smoking, %” in Table 1.
- The authors identify the paucity of data on asthma endotypes in the context of bronchiectasis-asthma overlap as a barrier to treatment decision-making, but do not present data on sputum inflammometry, which is a global benchmark for characterization and management guidance. This limits the translational applicability of the findings from the mouse experiments.
- The authors report a positive correlation between peripheral (serum) IL-17A and IL-17C in patients with bronchiectasis with or without asthma. It would be more informative to perform these analyses in patients with bronchiectasis alone, asthma alone, and with both bronchiectasis and asthma. The specific relevance of these findings in the context of ILC3 responses should then be demonstrated in patients with both bronchiectasis and asthma to support the contention that “IL-17C could serve as a potential therapeutic target for individuals of BA”.

MANUSCRIPT NCOMMS-24-60979
GENERAL COMMENTS.
This manuscript presents a clinical-translational study that addresses how bacterial colonization in patients with bronchiectasis and asthma alters immune signaling via the archetype Type 3 signaling pathway involving interleukin (IL)-17 cytokines, especially IL-17A and IL-17C. The data sets presented are extensive, consisting of data from humans, from cell and animal models. Taken together, the scientific basis for the manuscript and the presented conclusions is solid. Nevertheless, the results presented are important for the (improved) understanding of archetype immune signaling in patients with chronic airway disease and bacterial colonization, with future implications beyond asthma.
The scientific criticism relates mainly to the present focus on ILC 3 cells, a focus that leaves the expert reader with several unanswered questions regarding the role of Th17 and Tc17 cells. The mechanistic rationale for the critical role of IL-17A per se also deserves to be stated in a more precise manner, given its importance for this field of research (see also Specific comments below). Additional and important criticism relates to how the presentation of the underlying study is made, from a linguistic point-of-view. Key entities need to be handled in a more consistent manner than is now the case. Moreover, as the main text now stands, it is in need of editing by an expert in English. Once it is optimized in these respects, the manuscript is likely to become important for future research on chronic inflammatory airway disorders.
SPECIFIC COMMENTS.
A) Title: The title emerges as too definitive. Maybe "Evidence for IL-17C governing IL-17A pathogenicity..." would be better given that the focus is set mainly on ILC3 cells and not on additional sources of IL-17A? Another reason for this is that important evidence originates from experimental models and not humans in vivo.
B) Summary: The authors should make clear what evidence originates from humans and what evidence originates from experimental models. Apart from this, The scientific contents are fine but linguistic editing is needed.
C) Introduction:
1. Para 1 and 2: The text would benefit from the addition of information on Type 1 and Type 3-signaling and how these pathways relate to neutrophilic and eosinophilic inflammation. Here, key entities must be introduced and used in a more accurate and consistent manner than is now the case.
2. The entire study behind this manuscript study is based upon the role of IL-17A in mediating neutrophil accumulation in the lungs. Given this, a brief presentation of the basic evidence is appropriate, published in the original studies from Linden et al and from Kolls et al (summarized in Linden & Kolls, Immunity 2004; and in Linden & Dahlen, ERJ 2014). The original studies are also relevant for comments in the the results and the discussion (see below).
D) Results:
1. Table 2: Data sets on FEV1 and on ACT for healthy controls iare missing.
2. Text line 108: All FENO values are within the normal range, so the comment on a trend here doe s not seem meaningful.
3. Text line 165: These references are not adequate. See point C.2 for appropriate references.
4. Text line 281: The data set on MMP-9 emerges as important, not least given that this proteinase originates in part from neutrophils. The latter can be emphasized in the text here (as well as in the discussion and in the principal overview in Fig 8).
5. Apart from the above, the figures and tables seem adequate.
E) Discussion:
1. A general comment is that the text does not really make clear why the emphasis is set on ILC3 cells and not on other sourcces for IL-17A (such as Th17 or Tc17 cells).
2. Another general comment is that the discussion need to address the (potential) involvement of Type 1 signaling (via ILC 1 cells or via Th1 or Tc1 cells).
3. Text line 383: Figure 8 need to include MMP-9 given the current data and its relevance in neutrophilic inflammation in general (see also above).
4. Text line 413: Although this reviewer share the forwarded conclusions re. the current status of clinical evidence on inhibiting IL-17A signaling in asthma, the text here must be revised to make it easy to understand.
5. Text line 423: The presentation of published evidence on IL-17C i snow somewhat confusing and all publications on this may not be relevant for the current setting. This text can preferably be restricted to the most relevant publications.
6. Text line 460: The limitations of this study include the points forwarded as points E.1 and E.2 above.
7. Text line 469: The conclusion section should include comments on MP-9 as well (see above).
F) Methods:
1. Text line 610: The authors need to present the specific provider for each utilized assay, to make it possible for interested readers to reproduce data from this potentially important study.
2. Text line 644: The rationale for always using "two-sided significance" (regardless of pre-existing data and hypotheses) seem unclear and a rationale should be explained.
3. Except for the above, the methods seem adequately described.

references.

manuscript as instructed in point C.2 (Ref. 6, 7).

above comments.

We have re-written the part in Para 4 of the Discussion section in the revised manuscript
according to the above suggestion.

somewhat confusing and all publications on this may not be relevant for the
current setting. This text can preferably be restricted to the most relevant
publications.

Thank you for your constructive suggestion. To better convey the idea that the role of
IL-17C in regulating tissue inflammation has been controversial, the removal, addition
and a brief introduction of the most relevant publications have been made in Para 5 of
the Discussion section in the revised manuscript.
6. Text line 460: The limitations of this study include the points forwarded as points
E.1 and E.2 above.
Reply:
As indicated in E.1 and E.2, we have listed the potential involvement of type 1 and type
3 signaling as the fifth limitation in the revised manuscript.

well (see above).

As indicated in D.4, we have introduced neutrophil-derived MMP-9 and its role in
regulating IL-17C production to the conclusion section of the revised manuscript.

assay, to make it possible for interested readers to reproduce data from this
potentially important study.
Reply:

numerous antibodies for use in the experiment, we briefly introduced the providers of
these antibodies. Consequently, we have provided the specific providers of each utilized
assay in Supplementary Table 2 and indicated it at the end of the paragraph.
2. Text line 644: The rationale for always using "two-sided significance"

should be explained.
Reply:

clearly explained in the manuscript and we have supplemented the rationale in the
statistical analysis section of the revised version. Our study mainly concerns the
correlation analysis, one-way ANOVA, two-way ANOVA in terms of statistical analysis.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors’ response and rationale for inducing P. aeruginosa infection followed by allergic sensitisation to Ova in their murine model remains insufficiently justified. There has also been no attempt to examine the effects of the sequence of exposures experimentally where the authors could have investigated whether P. aeruginosa infection after the establishment of Ova-induced experimental asthma results in similar pathogenic interactions between IL-17C and ILC3s that potentiate IL-17A responses and a switch to the neutrophilic asthma endotype.
The additional information presented in Table 1 of the revised manuscript is informative, however, the potential influence of smoking history on the reported outcomes remains undiscussed.
There remains insufficient data to claim the study of asthma endotypes in bronchiectasis-asthma overlap. The absence of sputum inflammometry remains a critical limitation of the current study. This is inadequately justified by the authors’ and their reference to previous work showing that neutrophilic inflammation is the primary phenotype in asthma-bronchiectasis overlap, and the unscientific statement that those data are suggestive for the current study’s exploration of asthma endotypes in this overlap.
New data of correlations between serum IL-17A AND IL-17C in patients with bronchiectasis alone, asthma alone, and with both bronchiectasis and asthma are informative. However, these data show that positive correlations between IL-17A and IL-17C are also present in patients with asthma or bronchiectasis alone, yielding the same output across all groups in this comparison and weakening the authors’ contention that pathogenic IL-17C uniquely governs IL-17A pathogenicity and asthma endotype switching in bronchiectasis. Therefore, sputum inflammometry is required to provide some insight into the mechanistic disease endotype present in the patients with asthma alone. This also highlights the unsuitability of PBS/OVA mice to model the ‘asthma alone’ cohort in this study as these animals did not exhibit allergic induction of IL-17.

recruited the patients with primary bronchiectasis and coexisting asthma. Considering

underlying mechanisms involving in the asthma endotype within the context of

explore potential role of IL-17C in the endotype of asthma-bronchiectasis overlap, we

OVA/PA or OVA (Fig. d-p). However, potential factors affecting the asthma endotype
in an experimental asthma model followed by P. aeruginosa infection could be the time
interval between the last challenge and i.t. infection with P. aeruginosa accompanied
by duration of infection. Thus, the interesting scientific issue remains to be further
investigated in the future work.

The additional information presented in Table 1 of the revised manuscript is

bronchiectasis with asthma and airway inflammation is identified as an important
indicator for evaluation.
In the revised version of the manuscript, we supplemented P value of smoking rates
across the four groups in para 1 of the Result section, and further discussion concerning
the potential influence of smoking history on the reported outcomes was inserted into
para 2 of the Discussion section as follows: Notably, another potential factor that could
influence asthma endotype might be smoking history being associated with airway
inflammation. Nevertheless, the percentages of subjects with smoking history were
comparable across the groups involved in the study (P=0.4304). With limited sample
size, we couldn’t perform subgroup analysis of reported outcomes based on smoking
history among the patients of bronchiectasis with asthma.

bronchiectasis-asthma overlap. The absence of sputum inflammometry remains a
critical limitation of the current study. This is inadequately justified by the authors’
and their reference to previous work showing that neutrophilic inflammation is
the primary phenotype in asthma-bronchiectasis overlap, and the unscientific
statement that those data are suggestive for the current study’s exploration of

bronchiectasis with asthma may tend to be type 2-low asthma characterized by lower

orchestrating asthma endotype switching in bronchiectasis.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The authors have satisfactorily addressed my questions and comments with the support of new data, disclosures of the study’s limitations, and textual revision.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
GENERAL COMMENTS:
In this manuscript, the authors present a range of interesting and potentially important findings on key mechanistic aspects of the involvement of IL-17C in the immunopathology of the combined clinical phenotype of allergic asthma and bronchiectasis with bacterial colonization. In essence, all the needed data sets were in place already in the first version of the manuscript. However, although the authors have improved some of the reasoning, writing and grammar in their most recent revision, there is still need for improved scientific clarity. There is also some concern about the novel data set added (see point C below).
SPECIFIC COMMENTS:
Response and revisions relating to comments from
A) Reviewer 1: Satisfactory.
B) Reviewer 2: The authors do not responde to the criotical comments from this reviewer in a satisfactory manner. Reviewer 2 makes an important point regarding the seemingly artificial order of establishing the principal pathogenic events in the mouse model. This “order of events” is yet to be justified with clear and precise reasoning and writing, by the authors. Intuitively, it does seem less feasible that bronchiectasis including colonization with P aeruginosa would precede allergic asthma in real life. It seems more feasible that allergic asthma comes first and bronchiectasis later, as a feasible consequence of impaired immunity and chronic inflammation.
In their most recent revision of the manuscript, the authors fail to write about the above related matters in a clear and concise manner. For example, the statement on line 296 could just as well have been written in the opposite manner and be just as true (“Bronchiectasis is commonly reported in asthma patients”). This illustrates a more universal problem with the way the authors seem to reason and write – they fail to argue in a clear and structured manner why the chose the “experimental approach” that they did.
Given the above, it does become problematic that authors now have chosen to introduce a new and limited data set that fails to prove a matching impact on the specific immunopathology, using a revised model where the order of establishing principial pathogenic events is seemingly more relevant (ie. allergic asthma precedes bronchiectasis including colonization with P aeruginosa). It is hard to understand why the authors chose to include so few observations (small “n”) in their new data set, since this makes it hard to prove positive outcomes of immunopathological interest, when the alterations in cytokines and/or cells are small or variable. The small size of the novel material also makes it close to impossible to draw negative conclusions (due to risk for Type II error). Thus, by doing so, the authors weaken their own standpoint.
However, and importantly, given the current limitations of the scientific understanding of the clinical phenotype with both disorders (named "BA" in the manuscript), addressing the above is mainly a question of improving the way the authors present and discuss their evidence, although doubling the observations in their novel data set would clearly help in the current situation.
C) Reviewer 3: The response to this reviewer is acceptable but not fully satisfactory. The lack of basic clinical characterization of lung functon(spirometry) and symptoms (ACT) in the group of healthy subjects gives a poor impression in terms of clinical characterization, although it is understood that it is too late now to do anything about it now. Evidently, the authors cannot guarantee that their controls are truly healthy, although it seems feasible that this is the case. This reviewer thinks that this is acceptable, given that the problem is addressed as a “limitation” in the discussion.

## Abstract

The management of bronchiectasis-asthma overlap (BAO) is an important clinical issue to be addressed. Little is known regarding the endotype of BAO. Here we recruit patients with a primary diagnosis of bronchiectasis and co-existing asthma. The levels of interleukin (IL)-17C are positively correlated with the levels of IL-17A or group 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s) in peripheral blood samples from patients with BAO. An in vivo mouse model of Pseudomonas aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection followed by ovalbumin-induced asthma shows that IL-17C potentiates IL-17A expression via interacting with IL-17 receptor E in ILC3s. Additionally, ablation of Il17re in mice attenuates ILC3 responses and IL-17A-mediated asthma endotype switching towards neutrophilic asthma driven by P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection. Lastly, impaired epithelial barrier integrity by P. aeruginosa exposure is associated with IL-17C production in vitro. Collectively, our study implicates evidence for IL-17C governing IL-17A pathogenicity and promoting asthma endotype switching in bronchiectasis, implicating IL-17C as a potential therapeutic target for individuals with BAO.

---

## Introduction

Non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis and asthma exhibit the same degree of heterogeneity in terms of clinical manifestations and outcomes1–4. Based on the related immune-inflammatory pathways, asthma endotypes broadly cover three subgroups: type 2-high, type 2-low, and mixed endotypes. Type 2-high asthma is characterized by a predominance of eosinophils, while neutrophilic asthma is typical of type 2-low asthma5, where with release of cytokines such as interferon (IFN)-γ, interleukin (IL)-17 from T helper (Th)1, Th17 cells, group 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s) to recruit neutrophils and dampen the acquisition of eosinophils6–9, type 1 and type 3 immune responses predominate, leading to the suppression of type 2 immune responses10. In clinical practice, bronchiectasis and asthma frequently coexist, however, it is uncertain whether there is a cause-effect relationship between these two disorders. The overlap between bronchiectasis and asthma can be viewed as asthma-bronchiectasis overlap (ABO), and bronchiectasis-asthma overlap (BAO) with asthma accounting for 3-8% of bronchiectasis cases11–14, which are both clinical issues. The endotype of BAO has yet to be deciphered, and identifying the underlying mechanisms is therefore of key importance in precision medicine. Moreover, managing patients with BAO poses challenges, particularly when it comes to the use of corticosteroids. Inhaled corticosteroids and conventional asthma therapy are not regularly recommended for treating bronchiectasis, as the potential inhibition of host immunity and further increased risk of infections1,15. The conflicting treatment approach poses a significant challenge for healthcare providers. Literature on BAO is still scarce16,17, and the endotype of BAO remains to be fully defined, which has become a barrier to treatment decision-making. Furthermore, the lack of a mature animal model mimicking BAO has limited the availability of basic research data. Notably, Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common pathogen in the lower respiratory tract among bronchiectasis patients2,18, and it is also an independent risk factor for acute exacerbation in bronchiectasis16. And P. aeruginosa chronic infection model has been widely used in a repertoire of research on bronchiectasis19–21. Recent studies have indicated that colonization of nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae promotes the development of Th17-related neutrophilic asthma with glucocorticoid resistance22,23. Both P. aeruginosa and nontypeable H. influenzae belong to Gram-negative bacteria, but the precise asthma endotype which P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection drives remains unclear.

Innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) comprise group 1 ILCs (ILC1s), group 2 ILCs (ILC2s), and ILC3s, share the same features as three major effector CD4+ Th subsets, including Th1, Th2, and Th17 in the expression of transcription factors and cytokines, and act as pre-primed effector cells without de novo antigen-triggered effector cells differentiation24–26. The IL-17 family consists of six structurally related members (IL-17A, -17B, -17C, -17D, -17E, -17F). IL-17A and IL-17F are released by immune cells, mostly including ILC3, γδ T17, Th17 cells, and signal through IL-17 receptor A (RA)/IL-17RC and IL-17RA/IL-17RD complexes, and thus participate in host defense, inflammatory diseases, and autoimmune disorders partly by mediating neutrophil accumulation6,7. Other IL-17 members -IL-17B, IL-17C, IL-17D, IL-17E- contribute to regulating tissue inflammation by interacting with receptor complexes in epithelial cells or specific lymphocyte subsets27–30. However, the involvement of IL-17A, IL-17C, and ILC3s in the induction and development of endotypes within the context of BAO has not been deciphered.

In this work, we report a model of P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection followed by ovalbumin-induced experimental asthma mimicking BAO to investigate the underlying mechanisms involved in the endotype of BAO. This study indicates evidence for IL-17C governing IL-17A pathogenicity and promoting asthma endotype switching in bronchiectasis, implicating IL-17C as a potential intervention target for individuals with BAO.

---

## Results

Exposure to P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection drives asthma endotype switching towards neutrophilic asthma associated with Th17 cells and ILC3s
In the present study, 20 healthy controls (HC), 31 bronchiectasis patients, 30 asthmatics, and 31 patients with BAO were enrolled. And as shown in Supplementary Table 1, there was no obvious significance concerning the sex distribution and the percentages of participants with smoking history across the groups (P=0.1643, P=0.4304). Patients with BAO had worse lung function, as indicated by lower FEV1, FVC, FVC% pred values, lower scores on Asthma Control Test (ACT), lower levels of eosinophils and higher percentages of IgE to be below 100 compared to asthmatic patients, but there was no significance of FEV1% pred, FEV1/FVC, fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) values in patients with BAO (Supplementary Table 2). These characteristics suggested that BAO may tend to be type 2-low asthma with poor control.

As described in Fig. 1a, consistent with patients with a primary diagnosis of bronchiectasis and coexisting asthma within the context of BAO, we established a model of P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection through intratracheal (i.t.) instillation with P. aeruginosa-laden agar beads, followed by ovalbumin (OVA)-induced asthma to explore the specific endotype of BAO. Considering P. aeruginosa clinical strains are more efficient in building chronic infection compared with the PAO1 laboratory strain31, we confirmed a slower growth rate of 52D5 compared to another three existing clinical strains isolated from bronchiectasis patients in our lab (Supplementary Fig. 1a), and therefore adopting the 52D5 clinical strain in the subsequent experiments. To improve the efficiency of airway colonization with P. aeruginosa, we constructed the agar beads of diameter ranging between 100 and 200 μm31. Additionally, compared to sterile agar beads, P. aeruginosa-laden beads seemed denser as shown by visible single bacterial cells interiorly (Supplementary Fig. 1b). The establishment of chronic infection was successful as determined by recovery of more than 1000 colony forming units (CFUs) of P. aeruginosa from lung cultures32 at different time points post infection (Supplementary Fig. 1c). There was no significance of survival rates post infection between P. aeruginosa and P. aeruginosa/OVA (PA/OVA) group (Supplementary Fig. 1d).

Hematoxylin & eosin (HE) staining showed more marked peribronchial infiltration of inflammatory cells in treatment with OVA, PA, and PA/OVA compared to controls (Fig. 1b, c). Moreover, airway resistance was pronouncedly augmented in mice exposed to PA/OVA compared to mice exposed to phosphate-buffered saline/OVA (PBS/OVA) (Fig. 1d). And the levels of serum IgE and Th2-related cytokines IL-5, IL-13 in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) were reduced in mice exposed to PA/OVA compared to PBS/OVA, whereas the concentration of IL-17A was increased (Fig. 1e–h). Consistent with pathological presentations, the total cell numbers in BALF were elevated in mice exposed to OVA, PA, and PA/OVA (Fig. 1i). Furthermore, as depicted in Fig. 1j, the cell percentages and numbers of eosinophils whether in BALF or in lung tissues from PA/OVA group were consistently reduced compared to PBS/OVA group, whereas the cell percentages and numbers of neutrophils were elevated and the cell counts of alveolar macrophages (AM) were comparable (Fig. 1k–p). These findings suggested that exposure to P. aeruginosa chronic infection drove the asthma endotype switching towards neutrophilic asthma.

It is known that Th2 cells, together with ILC2s, contribute to eosinophilic asthma by producing IL-5 and IL-1333,34, while IL-17A-producing cells such as Th17, γδ T17, and ILC3 cells contribute to airway neutrophilia via IL-17A6,7,35,36. Consistently, compared to PBS/OVA exposure, PA/OVA exposure resulted in mitigated Th2 cell responses and upregulated Th17 cell responses (Fig. 2a–d). Additionally, through the assessment of ILCs based on the expression of transcription factors or cytokines, we found that the cell percentages and counts of ILC2s were consistently reduced in mice administered with PA/OVA in comparison with PBS/OVA-exposed mice, whereas ILC3s elevated (Fig. 2e–l). Meanwhile, with the determination of ILC2s based on cellular surface receptors, exposure to PBS/OVA increased the levels of ILC2s, whereas exposure to PA/OVA decreased (Supplementary Fig. 2a–c). The percentages of IL-17A-producing cells among CD3+CD4- lymphocytes which might be regarded as γδ T17 cells were increased in PA/OVA-treated mice compared to PBS/OVA-treated mice, but the cell numbers weren’t affected (Supplementary Fig. 2d). Additionally, mRNA level of Il17a was also significantly upregulated in lungs of mice administered with PA/OVA compared to PBS/OVA (Fig. 2m). Notably, we found no pairwise significance of the levels of Th1 and ILC1 cells among four groups (Supplementary Fig. 2e–g). Consistently, human data also indicated that patients with BAO presented higher levels of ILC3s compared to asthmatic patients or healthy participants (Supplementary Fig. 2h). Additionally, in line with the reported link of P. aeruginosa infection to Th2 responses37,38, our data showed raised TSLP in P. aeruginosa-infected patients with bronchiectasis or BAO, whereas no significance of CCL-17 levels was observed (Supplementary Fig. 2i, j). Thus, exposure to P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection led to a shift in asthma endotype towards neutrophilic asthma associated with IL-17A-producing Th17 cells and ILC3s.

IL-17A mediates asthma endotype switching towards neutrophilic asthma driven by P. aeruginosa chronic exposure
To understand the role of IL-17A in asthma endotype switching, an IL-17A neutralizing antibody (anti-IL17A) was administered to determine whether P. aeruginosa exposure-driven asthma endotype could be rescued as depicted in Fig. 3a. The administration of anti-IL17A attenuated peribronchial infiltrates of inflammatory cells and epithelium thickening induced by PA/OVA exposure, however, the effect was not observed in OVA group (Fig. 3b–d). Furthermore, IL-17A neutralization led to a mild increase in the levels of IgE, IL-5, IL-13, eosinophils, Th2 and ILC2 cells, whereas a significant decrease in the levels of IL-17A, total BALF cells, neutrophils, Th17 and ILC3 cells in the PA/OVA group (Fig. 3e–n and Supplementary Fig. 3d, f). Moreover, although the administration of anti-IL17A augmented the ratio of AM from mice treated with PA/OVA, the total numbers of AM, Th1, and ILC1 cells weren’t affected (Supplementary Fig. 3a–c, e). Taken together, these findings demonstrated that IL-17A mediated a shift in asthma endotype towards neutrophilic asthma driven by P. aeruginosa chronic lower respiratory tract infection.

Epithelial barrier integrity is impaired in a P. aeruginosa-exposed asthma model
Previous studies have reported the defective epithelial barrier integrity among patients with asthma39,40. Consistent with the mouse model, following pre-stimulation with P. aeruginosa, A549 cells were treated with OVA or IL-13 to resemble the airway epithelium within the context of BAO. We found that PA/OVA or P. aeruginosa/IL-13 (PA/IL13) exposure resulted in marked morphological changes in A549 cells from a typical multilateral paving stone-like appearance to a round or fusiform appearance accompanied by protrusions (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 4a). Furthermore, exposure to PA/OVA or PA significantly increased the intercellular permeability compared to OVA treatment (Fig. 4b). Moreover, the mRNA and protein levels of tight junction (TJ) markers, ZO-2, ZO-3, Claudin-18 and adhesion junction (AJ) marker, E-cadherin were remarkably decreased after PA/OVA or PA/IL13 exposure compared to OVA or IL-13 exposure (Fig. 4c–l).

Airway epithelium, as the first line of the physical barrier in the host, produces several alarmins such as TSLP41. Here we observed that exposure to PA/OVA or PA/IL13 augmented Tslp expression compared to the administration of OVA or IL-13 (Fig. 4m), which corresponds to the upregulated TSLP expression in human corneal epithelial cells exposed to P. aeruginosa infection42. In addition, the expression of ZO-3 and Claudin-18 located at the most apical part of neighboring epithelial cells were both decreased in the lungs of mice exposed to PA/OVA compared to OVA or their control (Fig. 4n, o and Supplementary Fig. 4b, c). Altogether, P. aeruginosa exposure resulted in a loss in epithelial barrier integrity characterized by the increased intercellular permeability and the decreased cell-cell adhesions.

The level of IL-17C positively correlates with IL-17A and is associated with the defective epithelial barrier integrity
Given the critical role of IL-17A in the model, we further explored the potential upstream regulator of IL-17A expression. Previous researches have demonstrated that IL-17C or IL-17B can regulate the activation of Th17 cells via a direct or indirect manner27,29,43,44. Moreover, IL-17B can inhibit eosinophilic inflammation by antagonizing IL-17E (IL-25) expression associated with type 2-high asthma45,46. We then examined the expression of IL-17 family members in P. aeruginosa chronic infection-driven asthma model. We found that Il17c expression was significantly upregulated in lung tissues of PA/OVA group compared with OVA group, whereas no significance of Il17b, Il17d, and Il25 mRNA expression was detected (Fig. 5a–d). Meanwhile, we observed significantly elevated expression of Il17c followed by remarkable upregulation in Il17a expression at the indicated time points in lung tissues of mice initially exposed to P. aeruginosa infection compared to their control (Fig. 5e, f). Furthermore, compared with OVA exposure, PA/OVA exposure elevated the concentration of IL-17C in BALF (Fig. 5g). Consistently, we found more productions of IL-17A and IL-17C in serum from patients with BAO than asthmatics (Fig. 5h, i). Notably, there was a consistently positive correlation between IL-17C and IL-17A levels (Fig. 5j). More importantly, IL-17C levels were also positively correlated with ILC3 levels in patients with BAO (Fig. 5k).

In line with animal and human data, IL-17C expression was upregulated in both BEAS-2B and A549 cells exposed to medium with a certain concentration of OVA following P. aeruginosa pretreatment (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b). Additionally, exposure to PA/OVA or PA/IL13 induced significantly elevated the expression of IL-17C compared to the treatment with OVA or IL-13 (Fig. 5l–o). MMP-9, secreted partly from neutrophils, is reported to modulate epithelial junction integrity47. Interestingly, exposure to PA/OVA or PA/IL13 expressed more Mmp9 than OVA or IL-13 administration (Fig. 5p, q). Notably, the pretreatment of MMP-9 inhibitor HY attenuated the impaired epithelial integrity and the upregulation of IL-17C expression induced by PA/OVA or PA/IL13 exposure (Supplementary Fig. 5c, d and Fig. 5r–u). Together, MMP-9 could modulate epithelial barrier integrity and thus regulating IL-17C expression.

Collectively, these data indicated that the levels of IL-17C positively correlated with IL-17A or ILC3 levels. Defective epithelial barrier integrity was associated with IL-17C production via MMP-9-dependent manner.

Ablation of Il17re inhibits IL-17A production in neutrophilic asthma driven by chronic infection with P. aeruginosa
It is known that IL-17C signals through IL-17RA/IL-17RE complex48. To investigate the potential role of IL-17C in asthma endotype switching, airway inflammation was evaluated in Il17re-/- mice. Exposure to PA/OVA exhibited milder peribronchial inflammatory infiltrates in Il17re-/- mice than wild-type (WT) littermates, but ablation of Il17re didn’t affect inflammatory infiltrates in the OVA group (Fig. 6a–c). Compared to WT littermates, CFU counts in the whole lung were markedly decreased in Il17re-/- mice exposed to PA/OVA or PA (Fig. 6d). Moreover, ablation of Il17re reduced the levels of IL-17A, total cell numbers, the cell counts of neutrophils, Th17 and ILC3 cells in mice exposed to PA/OVA, but failed to impact the levels of IL-5, IL-13, eosinophils, Th2 and ILC2 cells other than a mild increase in IgE levels (Fig. 6e–p and Supplementary Fig. 6b, c). In addition, total numbers of AM were not affected by ablation of Il17re (Supplementary Fig. 6a). Lastly, we found that interfering Il17c expression amplified the upregulated expression of Tslp in exposure to PA/OVA (Fig. 6q). Collectively, these data indicated that ablation of Il17re attenuated neutrophilic airway inflammation driven by P. aeruginosa chronic infection by preventing IL-17A production derived from Th17 cells and ILC3s.

IL-17C binds directly to ILC3s through interacting with IL-17RA-IL-17RE complex in lung tissues and potentiates IL-17A expression
To investigate the mechanisms by which IL-17C regulates IL-17A expression in ILC3s, we initially searched for the potential signaling targets in ILC3s. Interestingly, according to published RNA-seq data49, a significant increase in the expression of Il17re and Il17ra was supported in ILC3s of small intestine from WT mice, with Cd93 and Vipr2 expression being positive controls, but small amounts of transcripts expression of other IL-17R family members Il17rb, Il17rc, and Il17rd were observed (Fig. 7a). We observed that IL-17RE was situated on the surface of ILC3s and 98.9% among sorted ILC3s were RORγt+ (Fig. 7b–d). Next, we validated the binding capacity of IL-17A or IL-17C to ILC3s and identified more IL-17C or His labeling IL-17C binding to ILC3s, whereas ablation of Il17re attenuated the binding capacity (Fig. 7d, e). Furthermore, we found that following IL-17C treatment, ILC3s from C57BL/6 mice, compared to those from PBS-injected control mice, showed the elevated expression of IL-17A, whereas the comparable expression of the other transcripts associated with ILC3 function (Fig. 7f–h and Supplementary Fig. 7a–c). Moreover, we discovered that IL-17RE expression was comparable among ILC3 cell populations, whereas IL-17RE+ ILC3s expressed more IL-17A than IL-17RE- ILC3s in lung tissues (Supplementary Fig. 7d and Fig. 7i, j). Lastly, we found that IL-17RE was mostly expressed in T cells, macrophages/dendritic cells (MΦ/DC), and ILC3s (Supplementary Fig. 7e). Collectively, these findings indicated that IL-17C can interact with IL-17RE in ILC3s and potentiate ILC3 responses.
